newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: OECD emission plan would hit Australia badly-ABARE.
newsitem.headline: OECD emission plan would hit Australia badly-ABARE.

text.p: The OECD effort to reduce carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel combustion to 10 percent below 1990 levels by 2020 would cost Australia about A$9,000 per person in net present value terms, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said.

A 10 percent reduction would also cause large-scale cuts in Australia's output of non-ferrous metals, iron and steel and coal, the ABARE said in its latest editions of Current Issues, released on Monday.

Brian Fisher, executive director of Australia's official commodity forecasting agency, said the Australian cost would be about 22 times higher than the estimated loss for the average European and about six times that of an American.

Australia's heavy existing and future expected reliance on fossil fuels for power generation meant Australia would experience a more significant loss than most other countries if uniform emission abatement targets were adopted, he said.
Fossil fuel intensive processing was important in Australia's export profile and coal exports were important to the economy, Fisher said in a statement.

"ABARE estimates that uniform abatement targets will impose significant costs on Australian industry leading to a loss in competitiveness in key areas such as non-ferrous metals, principally aluminium, and iron and steel production," he said.

By 2020, an attempt to reduce emissions by 10 percent below 1990 levels would lead to an estimated fall in Australia's non-ferrous metals output of around 60 percent below the business as usual case and a fall in iron and steel production of 30 percent below the business as usual case, he said.
"Much of the policy debate has been about the extent to which emission reductions can be achieved using 'no regrets' (zero cost) policies," Fisher said.
But a policy that resulted in a 24 percent cut in coal output or a 60 percent cut in non-ferrous metals output would cause significant regional and sectoral adjustment costs.
ABARE estimates also pointed to significant economic costs to the Japanese economy from uniform emission abatement targets.

A more stringent target involving emission stabilisation at 15 percent below 1990 levels by 2010 and holding them there to 2020, a proposal similar to that put forward recently by the European Union (EU), would cost Japan around A$15,000 per person in net present value terms, Fisher said.
"These losses are significantly higher than those estimated for the U.S. or EU," he said.
Insistence on uniform emission reduction targets implied unequal economic burdens for countries of the Paris-based Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
The incidence of the burden changed as the targets became more ambitious, falling more and more heavily on countries such as Japan and Australia, he said.

"A demand for simplicity by some parties to the convention has led them to insist on uniform abatement targets," he said. "Such an approach does not lay the long-term foundation for an agreement that will be implemented wholeheartedly; that will provide a mechanism for signing on developing countries to undertake future commitments; or that will form the basis for introduction of innovative new policies such as tradeable emissions quotas."

The ABARE study follows political resistance by Australia to international pressure for it to agree to uniform reductions in emission of greenhouse gasses by developed countries after 2000. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
